guides.title: Motion, Forces & Newton's Laws
guides.summary: How and why objects move: the vocabulary of motion (position, velocity, acceleration), Newton's three laws, the common forces (gravity, normal, friction, tension), momentum, and how to solve real problems with free-body diagrams and worked examples.

sections.heading: The language of motion: displacement, velocity, acceleration
sections.body:
Mechanics begins with describing motion precisely (kinematics) before explaining it (dynamics). Define terms carefully:
• Position (x): where an object is along a chosen axis, measured from an origin, in metres (m). Position is a vector — it has direction (sign).
• Displacement (Δx = x_final − x_initial): the straight-line change in position, in metres. Distinct from distance, which is total path length travelled and is never negative.
• Velocity (v): rate of change of position, v = Δx/Δt, in metres per second (m/s). A vector: 60 km/h north differs from 60 km/h south. Speed is the magnitude of velocity (never negative).
• Acceleration (a): rate of change of velocity, a = Δv/Δt, in metres per second squared (m/s²). Acceleration occurs whenever speed OR direction changes — a car rounding a curve at constant speed is accelerating.
Sign convention matters: pick a positive direction first and stick with it. A ball thrown up with +15 m/s under gravity a = −9.8 m/s² slows, stops, and reverses; the negative sign carries all the physics.

sections.heading: The kinematic equations for constant acceleration
sections.body:
When acceleration a is constant, four equations relate the five quantities (initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a, time t, displacement s). Each equation omits one variable, so you choose the one lacking your unknown:
1. v = u + a·t   (omits s)
2. s = u·t + ½·a·t²   (omits v)
3. v² = u² + 2·a·s   (omits t)
4. s = ½·(u + v)·t   (omits a)
Units: u, v in m/s; a in m/s²; t in s; s in m. These only apply when a is constant (uniform acceleration), which includes free fall near Earth's surface where a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward (ignoring air resistance).
Worked example — braking car: a car travels at u = 20 m/s and brakes at a = −5 m/s². How far to stop (v = 0)? Use equation 3: 0² = 20² + 2·(−5)·s → 0 = 400 − 10·s → s = 40 m. How long? Equation 1: 0 = 20 + (−5)·t → t = 4 s. This is exactly the reasoning behind published stopping-distance tables.

sections.heading: Newton's First Law — inertia
sections.body:
Newton's First Law: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues at constant velocity (same speed, same straight-line direction), UNLESS acted on by a net external force. The tendency to resist changes in motion is called inertia, and mass (in kilograms, kg) is the quantitative measure of inertia — a loaded truck is harder to start or stop than a bicycle.
The key insight is that no force is needed to KEEP something moving; force is only needed to CHANGE motion. A hockey puck on frictionless ice glides forever. On real surfaces, friction is the hidden force that eventually stops things, which for centuries misled people into thinking motion needs constant pushing.
Everyday illustrations: a passenger lurches forward when a car brakes suddenly — the body's inertia keeps it moving while the car decelerates (this is why seatbelts exist). A tablecloth can be yanked from under dishes: the brief force does not act long enough to overcome the dishes' inertia. A frame of reference in which the First Law holds is called an inertial frame; an accelerating car is NON-inertial, which is why you feel 'thrown' even though no real force pushes you.

sections.heading: Newton's Second Law — F = m·a
sections.body:
Newton's Second Law quantifies how force changes motion: the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.
Formula: F_net = m·a
• F_net = vector sum of ALL forces acting (the net or resultant force), in newtons (N).
• m = mass in kilograms (kg).
• a = acceleration in m/s².
One newton is defined as the force that accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s²: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Force and acceleration always point the same direction. If several forces act, add them as vectors first, then divide by mass: a = F_net/m.
Worked example — pushing a crate: you push a 50 kg crate with 200 N while friction resists with 80 N. Net force = 200 − 80 = 120 N. Acceleration a = 120/50 = 2.4 m/s². If instead the crate is 100 kg, a = 120/100 = 1.2 m/s² — double the mass, half the acceleration for the same net force.
Weight is a force, not mass: weight W = m·g, where g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (also expressed as 9.8 N/kg). A 70 kg person weighs 70 × 9.8 = 686 N on Earth but the same 70 kg mass would weigh only about 116 N on the Moon (g ≈ 1.6 m/s²). Confusing weight (N) with mass (kg) is the single most common error in mechanics.

sections.heading: Newton's Third Law — action and reaction
sections.body:
Newton's Third Law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. If body A pushes on body B with force F, then body B pushes on body A with force −F (equal magnitude, opposite direction). Crucially, the two forces act on DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel each other.
Examples: When you walk, your foot pushes backward on the ground; the ground pushes forward on you — that reaction propels you. A rocket expels gas downward; the gas pushes the rocket upward (this works in the vacuum of space, needing nothing to 'push against'). A swimmer pushes water backward; water pushes the swimmer forward.
Common misconception: 'If forces are always equal and opposite, how does anything ever accelerate?' The answer is that the pair acts on two separate bodies. When a horse pulls a cart, the horse pulls the cart forward and the cart pulls the horse backward with equal force — but the horse ALSO pushes the ground, and the net force on the cart alone (harness tension minus friction) is what accelerates it. Always analyse the forces on ONE object at a time.

sections.heading: The everyday forces and free-body diagrams
sections.body:
Real problems combine several standard forces. Identify each and draw a free-body diagram — a sketch of the object as a dot with every force as a labelled arrow:
• Weight (gravity): W = m·g, always straight down toward Earth's centre.
• Normal force (N): the perpendicular push of a surface on an object resting on it; adjusts to prevent sinking. On flat ground with no vertical acceleration, N = W.
• Friction (f): resists sliding, parallel to the surface. Kinetic (sliding) friction f = μ_k·N; maximum static (not-yet-sliding) friction f_max = μ_s·N. The coefficient μ (mu) is dimensionless, typically μ_s ≈ 0.6 and μ_k ≈ 0.5 for rubber on dry concrete, but ≈ 0.1 for ice.
• Tension (T): the pull transmitted through a rope, cable or chain, always along its length.
• Applied and drag forces as relevant.
Procedure to solve: (1) draw the free-body diagram; (2) choose x and y axes; (3) write F_net = m·a for each axis; (4) solve. Worked example — box on a rope on a level floor: a 10 kg box is pulled by a horizontal rope with T = 40 N against kinetic friction with μ_k = 0.3. Weight = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N, so N = 98 N, friction f = 0.3 × 98 = 29.4 N. Net horizontal force = 40 − 29.4 = 10.6 N, giving a = 10.6/10 = 1.06 m/s².

sections.heading: Momentum, impulse and conservation
sections.body:
Momentum (p) is mass times velocity: p = m·v, in kilogram-metres per second (kg·m/s). It measures 'quantity of motion' and, like velocity, is a vector. Newton actually stated his Second Law in terms of momentum: F_net = Δp/Δt, force equals rate of change of momentum.
Impulse (J) is force applied over time: J = F·Δt = Δp, in newton-seconds (N·s). This explains safety design: to stop a moving mass you must remove a fixed amount of momentum, so spreading the change over a LONGER time reduces the peak force. A car crumple zone, an airbag, and bending your knees on landing all lengthen Δt and cut the force that would otherwise injure you.
Conservation of momentum: in any collision or interaction with no external net force, total momentum before equals total momentum after: m₁·u₁ + m₂·u₂ = m₁·v₁ + m₂·v₂. Worked example — recoil: a 3 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Before, total momentum = 0. After: (0.010 × 400) + (3 × v_rifle) = 0, so v_rifle = −4/3 ≈ −1.33 m/s (the rifle recoils backward). This same law governs rocket propulsion, billiard balls and spacecraft docking. Safety note in vehicles: because momentum change is fixed by your speed, the ONLY way to survive a crash better is to extend the collision time — hence never disable airbags and always wear a seatbelt.

sections.heading: Projectile Motion: When Gravity Works in Two Dimensions at Once
sections.body:
Every projectile — a thrown ball, a diver leaving a platform, a crate kicked out the back of a relief plane — obeys a deceptively simple trick: its horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent, and you can analyze them as two separate one-dimensional problems happening at the same time. Horizontally, with air resistance ignored, there's no force acting along that axis, so velocity stays constant: x = v₀ₓ·t. Vertically, gravity acts alone, so the same kinematic equations from constant acceleration apply: v_y = v₀y − g·t and y = v₀y·t − ½g·t². The only thing tying the two together is time — it's the shared clock both motions run on.

Take a humanitarian aid flight dropping a supply crate from an altitude of 500 m while flying level at 60 m/s (about 216 km/h). The vertical fall alone determines how long the crate is in the air: solving 500 = ½(9.8)t² gives t = √(1000/9.8) ≈ 10.1 s. In that time, the crate keeps moving forward at the plane's speed the whole way down (no engine, but no horizontal force to slow it either), covering x = 60 × 10.1 ≈ 606 m past the release point. That means the crew must release the crate more than half a kilometer before the target — a real calculation flight crews and forward observers have to get right, because misjudging that lead distance sends the payload well off the mark.

For a projectile launched at an angle θ above level ground and landing at the same height it started, two results are worth memorizing: the time of flight is t = 2v₀sinθ/g, and the range is R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g. That range formula peaks at θ = 45°, which is why 45° is the 'optimal' launch angle in idealized physics problems — though real athletes rarely use it. Mike Powell's still-standing 1991 long jump world record of 8.95 m was launched at roughly 20–24°, because a jumper's takeoff speed drops sharply at steeper angles (converting horizontal sprint speed into vertical lift costs you velocity), so the true optimum trades off angle against how fast you can still be moving when you leave the board.

sections.heading: Circular Motion and the Force That Keeps Things Turning
sections.body:
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating — a fact that trips up nearly everyone the first time they meet it, because 'constant speed' sounds like it should mean 'no acceleration.' But acceleration is any change in velocity, and velocity is a vector with direction as well as magnitude. Going in a circle means the direction is changing every instant, even if the speed isn't, and that requires a centripetal ('center-seeking') acceleration pointed directly at the circle's center: a_c = v²/r. By Newton's second law, that acceleration demands a real, physical net force pointed the same way — a centripetal force, F_c = mv²/r — supplied by whatever is actually available: string tension for a ball on a string, gravity for an orbiting satellite, and for a car rounding a curve, the friction between tires and pavement.

That last case has real stakes. A car taking a curve of radius 50 m at 15 m/s (54 km/h) needs a_c = v²/r = 225/50 = 4.5 m/s² of centripetal acceleration, which only friction can supply on a flat road. Since the maximum available friction force is μmg, the car needs a minimum coefficient of static friction of at least a_c/g = 4.5/9.8 ≈ 0.46 just to stay on the road. Dry asphalt typically offers μ around 0.7–0.9, giving comfortable margin — but wet pavement can drop below 0.4, and ice far lower, which is exactly why the same curve that's perfectly safe on a dry afternoon becomes a skid-off hazard in the rain: the required force didn't change, but the road's ability to supply it did.

Banked turns solve this more elegantly by tilting the road itself so that part of the normal force — not just friction — points toward the center. Racetrack designers exploit this aggressively: Daytona International Speedway's turns are banked at a striking 31°, letting cars corner at speeds that would fling them off a flat track's friction limit alone. A common misconception here is 'centrifugal force flinging you outward' — but in the car's frame there's no real outward force at all; it's your body's inertia trying to keep going in a straight line while the car curves out from under you, which only feels like being pushed outward.

sections.heading: The Two Faces of Friction: Why Things Stick, Then Slide
sections.body:
Friction turns out to have two distinct personalities. Static friction resists the start of relative motion between two surfaces already in contact, and it's self-adjusting — it grows to match whatever applied force it's opposing, up to a maximum value f_s,max = μ_s·N, where N is the normal force pressing the surfaces together and μ_s is the coefficient of static friction. Once the applied force exceeds that maximum and motion begins, friction drops to a lower, roughly constant value: kinetic friction, f_k = μ_k·N, with μ_k almost always somewhat smaller than μ_s. That's the physical reason a stuck drawer or a heavy dresser is hardest to get moving and then feels like it 'gives way' and slides more easily once it starts — you're crossing from the static regime into the kinetic one.

Typical coefficients vary enormously by surface pairing: rubber on dry concrete runs roughly μ ≈ 0.6–0.9 (why car tires grip so well), wood on wood around 0.2–0.5, steel on steel about 0.4–0.6, and waxed ski base on snow as low as 0.05–0.1 — deliberately engineered to be tiny. Ice against ice or a smooth sole can drop below 0.03, which is most of the reason winter falls happen so fast: the static threshold that would normally warn you with a 'catch' before slipping is barely there at all.

Strikingly, both coefficients depend only on the normal force and the material pairing — not on the apparent contact area. A brick dragged flat-side-down or edge-down experiences the same friction force, because at the microscopic level, real contact only ever happens at scattered high points (asperities), and pressing the same weight into a smaller apparent area just increases the pressure at those points proportionally. Leonardo da Vinci noted this and the proportionality to load in his notebooks around 1493 — centuries before Guillaume Amontons independently rediscovered and published the laws of friction in 1699, with Charles-Augustin de Coulomb refining the static/kinetic distinction in 1785. Da Vinci's manuscripts sat unpublished for so long that the field had to reinvent his insight from scratch.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions That Even Careful Thinkers Fall Into
sections.body:
The single most persistent misconception in mechanics is Aristotle's: that a constant force is needed to keep something moving, and that things naturally 'run down' to rest without one. It feels true because in ordinary experience, friction and air resistance are always quietly present, decelerating anything not actively pushed — a rolling ball does stop. But that stopping is the effect of an unbalanced force (friction), not the absence of one. Newton's first law says the opposite is true: absent any net force, motion continues unchanged forever. It took Galileo's thought experiments with increasingly smooth inclined planes — noticing that a ball rolled down one incline coasts further and further up an opposing incline as friction is reduced, seemingly trying to reach its original height regardless of the second incline's angle — to break Aristotle's fourteen-century hold on the question.

A closely related myth is that heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones. In a vacuum, all objects near Earth's surface accelerate downward at the same 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass, because the extra gravitational force on a heavier object is exactly canceled by its proportionally greater inertia (resistance to acceleration) — the two mass-dependences in F = mg and a = F/m cancel exactly. What actually makes a feather fall slower than a hammer in air is air resistance, a separate force entirely unrelated to gravity's pull, which is why the same feather and hammer famously fell together on the airless Moon during Apollo 15's 1971 demonstration.

Finally, people routinely conflate mass and weight, and speed with velocity. Mass is an intrinsic amount of matter (kilograms, unchanged anywhere in the universe); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (newtons, which would be about one-sixth as large on the Moon). Speed is a number; velocity is that number paired with a direction — which is precisely why an object can have constant speed while still accelerating, as in circular motion above.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: None of this requires a physics lab — most of it can be gathered from a hardware store, a hobby shop, or a kitchen drawer.
ingredients: A stopwatch or any smartphone's built-in timer/stopwatch app (reaction-time error matters, so time multiple repetitions, not one)
A metric tape measure or meter stick, for distances and heights
A small, dense weight — a large steel nut, a fishing sinker, or a padlock — to serve as a pendulum bob
About 1.5 m of sturdy string or thin cord, plus a fixed point to hang it from (a doorframe hook, a coat hook, a sturdy branch)
A protractor or a printed protractor template, for measuring launch/release angles
Marbles or steel ball bearings, and a smooth ramp or length of rigid plastic/PVC channel to roll them down
A bathroom scale (for your own mass) and a kitchen scale (for smaller masses, in grams)
A spring scale or luggage scale (reads out in newtons or can be converted from kilograms) for measuring applied forces directly
Optional: a smartphone accelerometer app, which turns the phone itself into a basic force/acceleration sensor

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Gravitational Acceleration With a Pendulum
sections.body: This is essentially Galileo's own method, refined — a homemade pendulum lets you measure g to within a percent or two of the accepted 9.8 m/s² using nothing but string, a weight, and a stopwatch.
steps: Tie your weight to the string so that the distance from the pivot point to the CENTER of the weight is exactly 1.000 m — measure this carefully, since it's the value you'll square in the final calculation.
Hang the string from a fixed point (doorframe hook, sturdy branch) high enough that the weight can swing freely without hitting the floor, walls, or furniture.

Pull the weight to one side so the string makes no more than about 15° with the vertical, then release it from rest. (Small angles matter — the simple pendulum formula below is only accurate for small swings.)
Using your stopwatch, time exactly 20 complete back-and-forth swings, starting the timer the instant you release the weight and stopping it after the 20th full return to the starting side.
Divide your total time by 20 to get the period T (the time for one full swing).
Calculate g using g = 4π²L / T², where L = 1.000 m and T is in seconds.
Compare your result to 9.8 m/s². A well-run trial should land within a few percent; if it's far off, check that you counted swings correctly and that the angle stayed small.

Repeat the whole procedure with L = 0.5 m and L = 1.5 m. You should get essentially the same g both times — direct proof that the period depends on length, not on 'how much gravity there is,' a common misconception this experiment quietly demolishes.

guides.title: Energy, Work, Power & Simple Machines
guides.summary: What energy is and its forms, the exact definitions of work and power, the conservation of energy, efficiency, and how the six simple machines multiply force through mechanical advantage — with formulas, worked calculations, and practical examples from levers to pulleys.

sections.heading: Energy: the capacity to do work, and its forms
sections.body:
Energy is the capacity to do work or cause change. Its SI unit is the joule (J), where 1 J = 1 newton-metre = 1 kg·m²/s². Energy comes in many interconvertible forms:
• Kinetic energy — energy of motion.
• Potential energy — stored energy of position or configuration (gravitational, elastic/spring, chemical, nuclear).
• Thermal energy — the kinetic energy of randomly moving particles (heat).
• Electrical, chemical, nuclear, radiant (light) and sound energy.
The great unifying principle is that these are all the same currency and convert into one another. A hydroelectric dam converts gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy of falling water → rotational energy of a turbine → electrical energy → (in your home) light, heat and motion. Other useful energy units: the calorie (1 cal = 4.184 J), the kilowatt-hour (1 kWh = 3.6 million J, the unit on your electricity bill), and the electronvolt (1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, used in atomic physics).

sections.heading: Work: force acting through a distance
sections.body:
In physics, work has a precise meaning: work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force.
Formula: W = F·d·cos(θ)
• W = work in joules (J).
• F = force in newtons (N).
• d = displacement in metres (m).
• θ = angle between the force and the displacement direction.
When force and motion are parallel (θ = 0°, cos 0° = 1), simply W = F·d. When force is perpendicular to motion (θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0), NO work is done — this is why carrying a heavy box horizontally at constant height does zero physics-work on the box (you tire only because your muscles burn chemical energy holding it, an internal process). Lifting the box vertically DOES do work against gravity.
Worked example: you push a lawnmower with a handle-force of 100 N at 30° below horizontal, moving it 20 m. Work = 100 × 20 × cos(30°) = 100 × 20 × 0.866 = 1732 J. Only the horizontal component of your push does useful work; the downward component just presses the mower harder into the ground.

sections.heading: Kinetic and potential energy formulas
sections.body:
Two workhorse equations quantify mechanical energy.
Kinetic energy (energy of motion): KE = ½·m·v²
• m = mass (kg), v = speed (m/s), KE in joules.
Because KE depends on v SQUARED, doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy — a car at 60 km/h carries four times the energy (and needs four times the braking distance) of the same car at 30 km/h. This is the physics behind speed limits.
Gravitational potential energy (energy of height): PE = m·g·h
• m = mass (kg), g ≈ 9.8 m/s², h = height above a chosen reference (m), PE in joules.
Worked example — a falling rock: a 2 kg rock is held 5 m up. Its PE = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J. As it falls, PE converts to KE. Just before impact (ignoring air resistance) all 98 J is kinetic: ½ × 2 × v² = 98 → v² = 98 → v ≈ 9.9 m/s. Notice this matches the kinematic result v = √(2·g·h) — the two approaches agree because they describe the same physics.

sections.heading: Conservation of energy and the work-energy theorem
sections.body:
The Law of Conservation of Energy is one of the deepest principles in all of science: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system is constant.
For mechanical systems with no friction: KE_initial + PE_initial = KE_final + PE_final. On a frictionless roller coaster, the sum of kinetic and potential energy is the same at every point — high and slow at the top, low and fast at the bottom.
The work-energy theorem states: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE = ½·m·v_final² − ½·m·v_initial². This links force directly to speed change.
When friction or drag is present, mechanical energy is not conserved as such — it is converted to thermal energy (heat). It is NOT lost; it becomes disordered. Worked example — a pendulum: released from height h = 0.20 m, a bob reaches maximum speed at the bottom of v = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.20) ≈ 1.98 m/s. If friction robs it of 10% of its energy each swing, the height it reaches on the far side falls to 0.18 m — the 'missing' 0.02 m × m × g of energy has warmed the air and pivot infinitesimally.

sections.heading: Power: the rate of doing work
sections.body:
Power measures how FAST work is done or energy is transferred — a strong person and a weak person can both lift the same load up the same stairs (same work), but the strong person doing it faster has more power.
Formula: P = W/t = E/t
• P = power in watts (W), where 1 watt = 1 joule per second.
• W or E = work or energy in joules; t = time in seconds.
A useful alternate form for a steady force moving something at speed v: P = F·v.
Units and benchmarks: 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W. A person climbing stairs steadily produces roughly 200 W; a sprinter briefly peaks near 1000–2000 W; a family car engine delivers 75–150 kW (100–200 hp).
Worked example — climbing stairs: a 60 kg person climbs a 3 m flight in 4 s. Work against gravity = m·g·h = 60 × 9.8 × 3 = 1764 J. Power = 1764/4 = 441 W ≈ 0.59 hp. Electricity billing uses power × time: a 2000 W (2 kW) heater run for 3 hours uses 2 × 3 = 6 kWh; at $0.15/kWh that costs $0.90.

sections.heading: The six simple machines and mechanical advantage
sections.body:
A machine does not create energy — it trades force for distance to make tasks easier. The ratio of output force to input force is the mechanical advantage (MA): MA = output force / input force = load / effort. A machine with MA = 4 lets you lift a load with one-quarter the force, but you must pull four times as far (energy in ≈ energy out).
The six classical simple machines:
1. Lever — a rigid bar pivoting at a fulcrum. Ideal MA = (effort arm length) / (load arm length). A crowbar, seesaw, and your forearm are levers.
2. Wheel and axle — a large wheel turning a small axle; MA = wheel radius / axle radius. Doorknobs, steering wheels, winches.
3. Pulley — grooved wheels with rope; MA ≈ number of rope segments supporting the load. A single fixed pulley (MA = 1) just changes direction; a block-and-tackle with 4 supporting ropes gives MA = 4.
4. Inclined plane (ramp) — MA = ramp length / height. Rolling a barrel up a 5 m ramp to a 1 m height gives MA = 5.
5. Wedge — two inclined planes back to back; axes, knives, chisels concentrate force to split.
6. Screw — an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder; large MA converts rotation into powerful linear force (jacks, clamps, bolts).

sections.heading: Efficiency, friction, and real machines
sections.body:
No real machine is perfect: friction always converts some input energy into wasted heat and sound. Efficiency measures how much useful output you get:
Efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) × 100%
Equivalently, efficiency = (actual MA / ideal MA) × 100%. A well-oiled pulley system might be 90% efficient; a rusty one 60%. A car's internal-combustion engine is only ~25–30% efficient (most fuel energy leaves as exhaust and radiator heat); an electric motor can exceed 90%.
Worked example: a ramp with ideal MA = 5 is used to push a 500 N barrel up. In theory you'd need 100 N, but friction means you actually push with 125 N. Actual MA = 500/125 = 4, so efficiency = (4/5) × 100% = 80%. The other 20% of your effort warms the ramp.
Practical applications and safety: (1) Lubrication (oil, grease, ball bearings) raises efficiency by cutting friction — but some friction is essential (brakes, tyres, walking would be impossible without it). (2) When using a lever or jack, remember the trade-off: you gain force but move a longer distance, so a car jack requires many turns. (3) Never overload a rated machine — a pulley or cable has a maximum working load; exceeding it risks sudden failure. (4) Energy conservation forbids perpetual-motion machines: any device claiming to output more energy than it takes in violates the First Law and cannot work.

sections.heading: Elastic Potential Energy and Hooke's Law: The Physics of Springs
sections.body:
A stretched or compressed spring stores energy just as surely as a lifted weight does — it's just stored in the deformation of the material rather than in height. For an ideal spring, the restoring force is proportional to displacement from its natural length: F = −kx, where k is the spring constant (in newtons per meter) and the minus sign shows the force always points back toward equilibrium. This is Hooke's Law, and the elastic potential energy stored in stretching or compressing the spring by x is PE_spring = ½kx² — the area under the triangular force-versus-displacement graph, exactly analogous to how the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.

Robert Hooke discovered this relationship around 1660 but, in the fiercely competitive scientific culture of the Royal Society, published it in 1676 only as a scrambled Latin anagram — 'ceiiinosssttuv' — to secure priority without revealing the actual discovery to rivals. He didn't reveal the solution, 'ut tensio, sic vis' ('as the extension, so the force'), until 1678.

A worked example with real stakes: a car's front suspension spring, with a typical spring constant around k = 25,000 N/m, gets compressed by 4 cm (0.04 m) hitting a pothole. The energy briefly stored is PE = ½ × 25,000 × (0.04)² = 20 J — energy that the shock absorber then has to dissipate as heat over the following second or so, rather than letting the car bounce that energy back out uncontrolled (which is exactly what happens when shock absorbers wear out, and the car bounces repeatedly after every bump instead of settling quickly).

sections.heading: Human Energy: Metabolism, Food Calories, and the Body as an Engine
sections.body:
The body is, in a very literal thermodynamic sense, an engine that burns chemical fuel to do mechanical work — and food Calories are simply energy units in familiar clothing. The dietary 'Calorie' (capital C, technically a kilocalorie) equals 4,184 joules. Muscles, however, are far from perfectly efficient converters: only about 20–25% of the chemical energy released from food during muscular exertion becomes useful mechanical work: the rest is released as heat, which is why hard exercise makes you warm and why your body sweats to shed that byproduct.

That efficiency figure produces a genuinely startling comparison. A typical jelly doughnut contains around 250 kcal, or 250 × 4,184 ≈ 1,046,000 J of chemical energy. If a 70 kg person's body converted that energy into climbing work at a 25% muscular efficiency, the usable mechanical work would be 1,046,000 × 0.25 ≈ 261,500 J. Since climbing height relates to work by W = mgh, the height reachable is h = W/(mg) = 261,500 / (70 × 9.8) ≈ 381 m. That figure isn't rounded for effect — it lands almost exactly on the 381 m roof height of the Empire State Building (not counting its antenna mast, which brings the total to 443 m). One doughnut, metabolized with perfect focus, is roughly enough chemical energy to climb New York's most famous skyscraper.

This same efficiency ceiling is why 'burning off' food through exercise is so much harder than eating it: a brisk hour-long walk might expend only 200–300 kcal of actual metabolic cost, a small fraction of a typical meal, because muscles simply cannot convert stored food energy into motion at anywhere near 100% efficiency — the rest becomes body heat, regulated away by sweating and increased blood flow to the skin.

sections.heading: Rotational Work, Torque, and Spinning Energy
sections.body:
Everything said about force, work, and energy has a rotational counterpart, and the translation is almost mechanical: force becomes torque, and linear speed becomes angular velocity. Torque, τ = r·F·sinθ, measures a force's twisting effectiveness around a pivot, depending on both the force's size and how far from the pivot (and at what angle) it's applied — which is exactly why a longer wrench handle makes a stuck bolt easier to turn: the same muscular force applied at r = 0.25 m instead of a stubby 0.10 m produces 37.5 N·m of torque instead of 15 N·m from an applied force of 150 N, more than doubling the twisting effect for identical effort. This is also why many passenger-car wheel lug nuts are specified to be torqued to roughly 100–140 N·m, and mechanics use long-handled torque wrenches specifically to reach that target without needing superhuman force.

Rotational kinetic energy follows KE_rot = ½Iω², where I is the moment of inertia — the rotational analog of mass, describing how a body's mass is distributed relative to the rotation axis (a solid disk of mass m and radius r has I = ½mr²; concentrating the same mass further from the axis, as in a bicycle wheel's rim, increases I and makes it 'store' more energy at the same spin rate).

This is the entire principle behind flywheel energy storage: a solid steel disk of mass 50 kg and radius 0.3 m, spun to 3,000 rpm (ω = 3,000 × 2π/60 ≈ 314 rad/s), has I = ½(50)(0.3)² = 2.25 kg·m² and stores KE = ½(2.25)(314)² ≈ 111,000 J — over 100 kilojoules held purely as spin, releasable on demand. Real transit systems and data-center backup power supplies use exactly this trick, spinning heavy flywheels up during braking or surplus power and drawing the energy back out later, all without a single chemical battery.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: This section's experiments run on ordinary household items plus a few cheap add-ons from a hardware or general goods store.
ingredients: A bathroom scale, to measure your own body mass
A tape measure or meter stick, to measure the vertical rise of a staircase
A stopwatch or a smartphone timer app
A set of stairs (at home, an apartment stairwell, or any public staircase you have safe access to)
A spring or a length of coil-spring material (an old ballpoint-pen spring, a slinky, or a small hardware-store extension spring) if you want to also verify Hooke's law
A kitchen scale that reads in grams, plus a set of known weights (bags of sugar/flour of labeled weight, or bottled water — 1 liter of water is almost exactly 1 kg) for the spring experiment
A ruler taped alongside the hanging spring, to read extension distances

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Your Own Horsepower on a Staircase
sections.body: This is the classic 'power lab' — a direct, satisfying way to attach a real wattage number to your own physical effort, using nothing but stairs and a stopwatch.
steps: Weigh yourself on a bathroom scale in kilograms (if it reads in pounds, divide by 2.205) to get your mass m.

Measure the total vertical rise of your staircase: either measure the height of one riser (typically 0.15–0.19 m) with a tape measure and multiply by the number of steps, or measure the total floor-to-floor height directly with a tape measure alongside the stairwell.

Warm up briefly, then have someone start a stopwatch the instant you begin, and stop it the instant you reach the top — climb at a hard but safe pace, using the handrail, without leaping steps dangerously.
Record your climb time t in seconds.
Calculate the mechanical power output: P = mgh / t, where g = 9.8 m/s².

Convert to horsepower by dividing by 746 (1 hp = 746 W) to see what fraction of a 'horsepower' your legs briefly produced — most people land somewhere between 0.3 and 0.6 hp in a hard sprint up a flight of stairs, a number completely out of reach for sustained effort (your body can only average roughly 100 W, about 0.13 hp, over an hour of continuous work).

Try it again at a slow, comfortable walking pace up the same stairs and recalculate — you did exactly the same amount of WORK both times (same mgh), but a dramatically different amount of POWER, since power is work divided by time. This is the clearest possible demonstration that work and power are not the same quantity.

guides.title: Electricity & Magnetism
guides.summary: Electric charge, current, voltage and resistance; Ohm's law and how to calculate them; series versus parallel circuits; electrical power and safety; magnetism, electromagnets, and how motors and generators turn electricity and motion into one another — with formulas, worked circuits, and life-saving safety rules.

sections.heading: Electric charge: the source of all electrical phenomena
sections.body:
Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter, carried by subatomic particles. There are two kinds: positive (protons, in the atomic nucleus) and negative (electrons, orbiting the nucleus). The rule is simple: like charges repel, opposite charges attract. The unit of charge is the coulomb (C); one electron carries −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so it takes about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons to make one coulomb.
Most objects are neutral (equal positive and negative charge). Rubbing certain materials transfers electrons — this is static electricity. Rub a balloon on hair: electrons move to the balloon (now negative), leaving the hair positive; they attract, and the hair stands up. A lightning strike is a massive static discharge when charge separation between cloud and ground grows until air breaks down.
Coulomb's Law gives the force between two point charges: F = k·q₁·q₂/r², where F is force (N), q₁ and q₂ are the charges (C), r is their separation (m), and k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² (Coulomb's constant). Like gravity it is an inverse-square law: double the distance, quarter the force. Unlike gravity, it can push (repel) as well as pull.

sections.heading: Current, voltage and resistance defined
sections.body:
Three quantities describe any circuit. A plumbing analogy helps: voltage is like water pressure, current is like flow rate, resistance is like pipe narrowness.
• Current (I): the rate of flow of electric charge, I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A). One ampere = one coulomb per second. Current flows through a component.
• Voltage (V), or potential difference: the energy given to each coulomb of charge by a source, measured in volts (V). One volt = one joule per coulomb. Voltage is measured ACROSS a component (it is a difference between two points). A battery's voltage is its 'push'.
• Resistance (R): opposition to current flow, measured in ohms (Ω). Thin, long, hot wires of poor conductors have high resistance; thick, short, cool wires of copper have low resistance.
Conventional current is defined as flowing from + to − (the direction positive charge would move), even though in metal wires it is actually electrons drifting the opposite way — a historical convention that works consistently. Note the drift speed of electrons is astonishingly slow (millimetres per second), yet the electrical signal travels near light speed, because the whole 'column' of electrons pushes at once, like water in a full pipe.

sections.heading: Ohm's Law and worked circuit calculations
sections.body:
Ohm's Law is the central relationship of circuit analysis: voltage equals current times resistance.
Formula: V = I·R
• V = voltage in volts (V).
• I = current in amperes (A).
• R = resistance in ohms (Ω).
Rearranged: I = V/R (current for a given voltage and resistance) and R = V/I (resistance from measured voltage and current).
Worked example 1 — LED with a resistor: you have a 9 V battery and want 20 mA (0.020 A) through an LED that drops 2 V, so 7 V must be dropped across a series resistor. R = V/I = 7/0.020 = 350 Ω. You would choose the nearest standard value (e.g. 360 Ω) to protect the LED from burning out.
Worked example 2 — household appliance: a heater draws 10 A on a 240 V supply. Its resistance R = V/I = 240/10 = 24 Ω. Ohm's Law holds for 'ohmic' materials (metals at constant temperature); components like diodes, LEDs, and filament bulbs are non-ohmic (their resistance changes with conditions), so the law is an approximation for them, but it remains the everyday tool for sizing resistors and predicting currents.

sections.heading: Series and parallel circuits
sections.body:
Components can be wired two fundamental ways, and the difference is crucial.
Series circuit — components in a single loop, one after another. The SAME current flows through all; voltages ADD; resistances ADD: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …. Drawback: if one component fails open (like an old Christmas light), the whole chain goes dark. Total resistance is always larger than any single resistor.
Parallel circuit — components on separate branches sharing the same two nodes. The SAME voltage is across all; currents ADD; resistances combine as reciprocals: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + …. Total resistance is always SMALLER than the smallest branch. Home wiring is parallel so every outlet gets the full 120 V (or 230 V) and one appliance switching off does not kill the others.
Worked example — two resistors: R₁ = 6 Ω and R₂ = 3 Ω. In series: R_total = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. In parallel: 1/R_total = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6, so R_total = 2 Ω. Note the parallel total (2 Ω) is less than the smaller resistor (3 Ω) — adding a parallel path always increases current-carrying capacity and lowers resistance.

sections.heading: Electrical power and energy cost
sections.body:
Electrical power is the rate at which a circuit converts electrical energy into other forms (heat, light, motion).
Primary formula: P = V·I
• P = power in watts (W), V = voltage (V), I = current (A).
Using Ohm's Law this becomes two equivalent forms: P = I²·R and P = V²/R, handy when you know current-and-resistance or voltage-and-resistance instead.
Worked example: a 60 W light bulb on a 120 V supply draws I = P/V = 60/120 = 0.5 A and has resistance R = V²/P = 120²/60 = 240 Ω.
Energy and money: energy = power × time. Electricity is billed in kilowatt-hours (kWh): a 1500 W (1.5 kW) space heater run 5 hours a day uses 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 kWh/day; over a 30-day month that is 225 kWh, and at $0.15/kWh costs about $34/month. This is why high-wattage, always-on devices dominate power bills, and why efficiency labels matter. Practical note: the I²·R form explains why long-distance power lines use very high voltage — for a given power, higher voltage means lower current, which slashes the I²·R heating losses in the wires (halving current cuts line loss to a quarter).

sections.heading: Magnetism and electromagnetism
sections.body:
Magnetism and electricity are two faces of one force. A magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel, opposite poles attract, and (unlike electric charge) poles always come in pairs — cut a magnet in half and each piece has its own N and S. Magnets create a magnetic field, a region where magnetic force acts, visualised by field lines running from N to S outside the magnet. Earth itself is a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle aligns roughly north-south.
The pivotal discovery (Ørsted, 1820) is that an electric current creates a magnetic field. A straight wire carrying current is encircled by a magnetic field; coil that wire into a solenoid and wrap it around an iron core and you get an electromagnet — a magnet you can switch on and off and whose strength you control by the current and number of turns. Electromagnets run scrapyard cranes, doorbells, relays, hard drives and MRI machines.
Electromagnetic induction (Faraday, 1831) is the reverse: a CHANGING magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage in it. Move a magnet in and out of a coil and current flows. This one principle underlies nearly all electricity generation on Earth — Faraday's law states the induced voltage is proportional to how fast the magnetic flux changes.

sections.heading: Motors, generators, and electrical safety
sections.body:
Two devices exploit the electricity-magnetism link and are essentially each other run backwards:
• Electric MOTOR — converts electrical energy into mechanical rotation. Current through a coil in a magnetic field feels a force (the motor effect), spinning the coil. Motors drive fans, pumps, drills, electric vehicles and appliances.
• GENERATOR (or dynamo) — converts mechanical rotation into electricity by induction. Spin a coil in a magnetic field (turned by falling water, steam, wind, or a diesel engine) and it generates voltage. Power stations are giant generators.
Electrical safety — these rules can save your life:
• It is CURRENT, not voltage alone, that harms: as little as 100 milliamps (0.1 A) through the chest can cause fatal heart fibrillation. Because I = V/R and dry skin has high resistance (~100,000 Ω) while wet skin drops to ~1,000 Ω, water dramatically raises the danger — never handle electrical devices with wet hands or near water.
• Fuses and circuit breakers protect against too much current: they melt or trip and cut power before wires overheat and start fires. Never replace a fuse with a higher rating or a coin.
• The earth/ground wire provides a safe path for fault current, and a GFCI/RCD outlet cuts power within milliseconds if it detects current leaking to ground (as through a person) — required by code near sinks and bathrooms.
• Treat every wire as live until proven dead. For household mains and especially high-voltage lines, do not attempt repairs without proper training, and never assume a downed power line is safe.

sections.heading: Coulomb's Law and the Electric Field: Force at a Distance
sections.body:
Charles-Augustin de Coulomb established in 1785, using a delicate torsion balance of his own design, exactly how the electric force between two point charges depends on their size and separation: F = k·q₁q₂/r², where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² (the Coulomb constant) and r is the distance between the charges. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and the force falls off with the square of distance — meaning doubling the separation cuts the force to a quarter, not a half, a relationship shared with Newton's law of gravity.

Because it's often more useful to describe the 'influence' a charge projects into the space around it independent of what other charge might show up, physicists define the electric field E at a point as the force per unit charge that would be felt there: E = F/q, which for a point charge Q works out to E = kQ/r². Field lines — an invention of Michael Faraday's — visualize this: they point in the direction a small positive test charge would be pushed, radiating outward from positive charges and converging into negative ones, with density representing field strength.

A worked example shows just how large that constant k really is compensating for: two charges of just 1 microcoulomb each (1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C — roughly the charge a balloon might pick up from vigorous rubbing on hair, though real static charges are usually far smaller), separated by 1 meter, exert F = (8.99 × 10⁹)(10⁻⁶)(10⁻⁶)/(1)² ≈ 8.99 × 10⁻³ N — about 9 millinewtons, roughly the weight of a small paperclip. It takes an enormous k to make even microscopic charges produce measurable force, which is exactly why it took until 1909 — via Robert Millikan's famous oil-drop experiment, balancing gravity against the electric force on charged oil droplets suspended between charged plates — to isolate and measure the charge of a single electron, e ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, a result that won Millikan the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.heading: Capacitors: Storing Electric Charge — and Real Danger
sections.body:
A capacitor is a device built specifically to store electric charge and the energy that comes with it, typically two conductive plates separated by a thin insulating gap. Its defining property is capacitance, C = Q/V (charge stored per volt applied), measured in farads — a unit so large that practical capacitors are usually specified in microfarads (μF, millionths) or picofarads (pF, trillionths). The energy stored is U = ½CV², growing with the square of applied voltage just like a stretched spring's energy grows with the square of displacement — not a coincidence, since both derive from integrating a linearly increasing quantity (charge or displacement) against a linearly increasing opposing quantity (voltage or restoring force).

This stored energy is genuinely useful — and genuinely hazardous. A disposable camera's flash circuit charges a modest 150 μF capacitor to around 300 V to fire the flash tube; the stored energy is U = ½(150 × 10⁻⁶)(300)² = 6.75 J. That's a small number next to a car battery's output, but delivered in a fraction of a millisecond through skin contact, it's enough to produce a genuinely painful — and startling — shock, which is why anyone who opens up disposable camera electronics is warned to deliberately discharge the capacitor first (through a resistor, never a direct short) rather than assume it's safe once the battery is removed. The same principle scales up dramatically in defibrillators, which intentionally store on the order of 100–360 J to deliver a therapeutic shock through the heart — a stark reminder that a capacitor can hold a dangerous charge long after the power source that charged it is gone, unlike a simple wire circuit that goes dead the instant the battery is disconnected.

sections.heading: AC, DC, and the War of the Currents
sections.body:
Electricity comes in two fundamentally different flavors: direct current (DC), where charge flows steadily in one direction (as from a battery), and alternating current (AC), where the current periodically reverses direction — in most of the world's electrical grids, 50 or 60 times per second. The reason nearly all long-distance power transmission uses AC comes down to one device: the transformer, which can only step voltage up or down using a changing (alternating) magnetic field — something DC, with its constant current, cannot provide.

That matters enormously because power lost to a transmission line's resistance is P_loss = I²R — it depends on the SQUARE of current, not on the power being delivered. Since P = IV, delivering a fixed amount of power at a higher voltage requires proportionally less current, which shrinks I²R losses dramatically. Consider sending 100,000 W of power down a line with just 1 Ω of resistance: at a household-scale 240 V, the required current is I = P/V ≈ 417 A, and the loss would be I²R ≈ 173,900 W — MORE than the power being delivered, which is exactly why you never see this attempted; the voltage would simply collapse before the load received meaningful power. Step the transmission voltage up to 100,000 V (100 kV) instead, and the same 100,000 W only requires I = 1 A, dropping the loss to a negligible 1 W. This single relationship is why power grids transmit at extremely high voltages over long distances and only step back down to safe household voltages near the point of use.

This is also why AC won a genuine, high-stakes commercial battle in the 1880s and 90s — the 'War of the Currents' — between Thomas Edison, who had built his empire on DC generation and distribution, and George Westinghouse, backed by Nikola Tesla's AC induction motor and transformer patents. AC's ability to transmit efficiently over long distances proved decisive, most visibly when the Adams Power Station at Niagara Falls, built to a Westinghouse/Tesla AC design and completed in 1895, began transmitting hydroelectric power over 20 miles to Buffalo, New York — a scale of long-distance electrification that DC-only systems of the era simply could not achieve.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: A basic circuits kit is inexpensive and widely available from any electronics or hobbyist supply store, and everything below is reusable indefinitely.
ingredients: A solderless breadboard (a plastic board with a grid of spring clips for building circuits without soldering)
A digital multimeter (any $15-30 model with voltage, current, and resistance/continuity settings)
A battery holder with fresh AA batteries, or a single 9V battery with a snap connector
An assortment pack of resistors covering a range of values (commonly sold as a 'resistor kit' with values from a few ohms to several megaohms)
A handful of jumper wires or breadboard wire, plus a couple of alligator-clip test leads
One or two small LEDs (useful bonus for observing polarity and voltage drop, though not required for the core exercise)
Optional: a small electrolytic capacitor (10-100 μF) if you want to extend the exercise to charge/discharge behavior

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build a Circuit and Verify Ohm's Law Yourself
sections.body: This turns the abstract V = IR relationship into something you measure with your own hands, using a battery, a couple of resistors, and a multimeter.
steps: Set your multimeter to measure resistance (Ω) and directly test one resistor from your kit — confirm its value against the color-code printed on it (or its labeled value if pre-marked) before building anything.
On the breadboard, connect the battery's positive terminal through the resistor to the negative terminal, forming a simple closed loop — this is your basic series circuit.
Switch the multimeter to DC voltage mode and measure the voltage across the battery terminals directly (record it — a fresh 9V battery often reads slightly above 9V).

Without disconnecting anything, switch the multimeter to DC current mode, break the circuit at one point, and insert the meter in series (current must flow THROUGH the meter, unlike voltage which is measured ACROSS a component) to read the circuit current in milliamps.

Calculate resistance from your own readings: R = V/I, and compare it to the resistor's labeled value — they should match closely (small differences come from the battery's own tiny internal resistance and the resistor's manufacturing tolerance, often ±5%).
Now add a second resistor in SERIES (end to end, in the same loop) and remeasure total current; verify that total resistance R_total = R₁ + R₂ by recomputing R = V/I_new.

Rebuild with the two resistors in PARALLEL instead (both connected across the same two points, giving current two separate paths) and remeasure; verify that 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ — you should measure a LOWER total resistance and HIGHER total current than either single resistor alone, which surprises most people the first time they see it.

Safety note: keep this experiment to low-voltage battery power only (9V or less) — never attempt to probe household mains wiring or outlets with a multimeter unless you are a trained, licensed electrician, since household current is genuinely lethal.

guides.title: Heat & Thermodynamics
guides.summary: Temperature versus heat, the three modes of heat transfer, specific heat and phase changes with real calculations, thermal expansion, the gas laws, and the four laws of thermodynamics that govern engines, refrigerators, and why perpetual motion is impossible.

sections.heading: Temperature vs heat: two different things
sections.body:
People use 'heat' and 'temperature' interchangeably, but physics draws a sharp line.
• Temperature is a measure of the AVERAGE kinetic energy of the particles in a substance — how fast, on average, its molecules jiggle. It does not depend on how much substance you have. Units: Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F), and the SI absolute scale Kelvin (K).
• Heat (Q) is the ENERGY transferred between objects because of a temperature difference, measured in joules (J). Heat always flows spontaneously from hotter to colder, never the reverse on its own.
Analogy: a lit match has a very high temperature but little total heat energy (few particles); a warm bathtub has a lower temperature but far more total thermal energy (vastly more particles). Dropping the match in the tub barely warms it.
Temperature conversions: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32; °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9; K = °C + 273.15. Absolute zero (0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F) is the theoretical point where particle motion is minimised — it can be approached but never reached. Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F, 273.15 K) and boils at 100 °C (212 °F, 373.15 K) at sea-level pressure.

sections.heading: The three modes of heat transfer
sections.body:
Heat moves from hot to cold by three mechanisms; most real situations combine them.
1. Conduction — heat transfer through direct contact, as fast-vibrating particles jostle their slower neighbours. It dominates in solids, especially metals. Metals feel colder than wood at the same temperature because they conduct heat away from your hand faster. The rate depends on the material's thermal conductivity (copper ~400 W/m·K conducts ~2000× better than air ~0.024 W/m·K), the area, the temperature difference, and inversely on thickness. Insulation (fibreglass, foam, still air, down) works by trapping air, a poor conductor.
2. Convection — heat carried by the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas). Heated fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises while cooler fluid sinks, creating a convection current. This is how a radiator warms a whole room, how ocean currents and weather form, and why hot air rises. Forced convection (a fan, a pump) speeds it up.
3. Radiation — heat transferred as electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared), requiring NO medium; it crosses the vacuum of space. Every object radiates according to its temperature; the Sun warms Earth entirely by radiation. Dark, matte surfaces absorb and emit radiation well; shiny, light surfaces reflect it — which is why survival blankets are silver and why light-coloured clothing is cooler in summer. A vacuum flask (thermos) defeats all three: a vacuum gap stops conduction and convection, and silvered walls reflect radiation.

sections.heading: Specific heat capacity and calorimetry
sections.body:
Different substances need different amounts of energy to warm up. Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy needed to raise 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 degree Celsius (or 1 Kelvin).
Formula: Q = m·c·ΔT
• Q = heat energy in joules (J).
• m = mass in kilograms (kg).
• c = specific heat capacity in J/(kg·°C).
• ΔT = temperature change in °C (or K — the size of one degree is identical on both scales).
Water has an exceptionally high specific heat, c = 4186 J/(kg·°C), meaning it resists temperature change strongly. This moderates coastal climates, makes water an excellent coolant and radiator fluid, and is why a swimming pool stays cool on a hot day while the surrounding pavement scorches. By contrast iron is ~450 and aluminium ~900 J/(kg·°C).
Worked example: to heat 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C (ΔT = 80 °C): Q = 2 × 4186 × 80 = 669,760 J ≈ 670 kJ. If your kettle supplies 2000 W (2000 J/s), the minimum boil time is 669,760/2000 ≈ 335 s ≈ 5.6 minutes (longer in reality due to heat losses). This same Q = m·c·ΔT calculation lets you size heaters, predict cooling, and balance heat exchanges in calorimetry, where heat lost by a hot object equals heat gained by a cold one.

sections.heading: Phase changes and latent heat
sections.body:
When a substance changes state (solid ↔ liquid ↔ gas), its temperature stays CONSTANT even as energy pours in or out — the energy goes into breaking or forming molecular bonds, not into speeding up particles. This hidden energy is latent heat.
Formula: Q = m·L
• Q = heat energy (J), m = mass (kg), L = specific latent heat (J/kg).
Two kinds: latent heat of fusion (melting/freezing) and latent heat of vaporisation (boiling/condensing). For water, L_fusion = 334,000 J/kg and L_vaporisation = 2,260,000 J/kg. Vaporisation takes about 6.8× more energy than melting because separating molecules into a gas requires breaking bonds completely.
Worked example — melting ice then boiling it: to convert 1 kg of ice at 0 °C to steam at 100 °C takes three stages: (1) melt: 1 × 334,000 = 334,000 J; (2) heat water 0→100 °C: 1 × 4186 × 100 = 418,600 J; (3) vaporise: 1 × 2,260,000 = 2,260,000 J. Total ≈ 3,012,600 J ≈ 3 MJ, and the vast majority is the final boiling step.
Practical consequences: (1) Sweating cools you because evaporating sweat draws its huge latent heat from your skin. (2) Steam burns are far worse than boiling-water burns at the same 100 °C because condensing steam dumps 2.26 MJ/kg of latent heat into your skin — a critical safety warning around kettles and pressure cookers. (3) Ice keeps drinks cold efficiently because melting absorbs 334 kJ/kg without the water even warming.

sections.heading: Thermal expansion
sections.body:
Almost all materials expand when heated and contract when cooled, because warmer particles vibrate more vigorously and push each other farther apart. For a solid rod, linear expansion is: ΔL = α·L₀·ΔT, where ΔL is the length change (m), L₀ the original length (m), ΔT the temperature change (°C), and α the coefficient of linear expansion (per °C) — for steel α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶/°C, aluminium ≈ 23 × 10⁻⁶/°C, glass ≈ 9 × 10⁻⁶/°C.
Worked example: a 100 m steel bridge span heated by 40 °C expands by ΔL = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 40 = 0.048 m = 4.8 cm. That is why bridges have expansion joints (the finger-like gaps you drive over) and why railway tracks and concrete pavements have gaps — without them, thermal stress buckles them in summer.
Everyday applications: a stuck metal jar lid loosens under hot water because the metal expands more than the glass; thermometers work by the expansion of mercury or coloured alcohol up a thin tube; a bimetallic strip (two metals with different α bonded together) bends when heated and is the switch inside thermostats and older thermal fuses. Water is a famous anomaly: below 4 °C it EXPANDS as it cools toward freezing, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats — a quirk that lets fish survive under a frozen lake's surface.

sections.heading: The gas laws
sections.body:
Gases respond dramatically to changes in pressure, volume and temperature. Three simple laws (all requiring ABSOLUTE temperature in Kelvin) combine into one:
• Boyle's Law (constant temperature): P·V = constant — pressure and volume are inversely related. Squeeze a gas to half its volume and its pressure doubles.
• Charles's Law (constant pressure): V/T = constant — volume is proportional to absolute temperature. Heat a balloon and it swells.
• Gay-Lussac's Law (constant volume): P/T = constant — heat a sealed rigid can and its pressure rises (why aerosol cans warn against fire).
Combined gas law: (P₁·V₁)/T₁ = (P₂·V₂)/T₂. The full ideal gas law is PV = nRT, where P is pressure (Pa), V volume (m³), n the amount in moles, T absolute temperature (K), and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) the universal gas constant.
Worked example — a warming tyre: a car tyre holds air at P₁ = 200 kPa and T₁ = 290 K (17 °C). After highway driving the air heats to T₂ = 320 K (47 °C) at essentially constant volume. New pressure P₂ = P₁ × T₂/T₁ = 200 × 320/290 ≈ 221 kPa. This ~10% rise is why you check tyre pressures cold. Safety note: NEVER heat a sealed container of gas or liquid — the pressure can rise until it bursts violently; this is the danger of throwing aerosol cans or sealed bottles into a fire.

sections.heading: The laws of thermodynamics
sections.body:
Four laws govern all energy and heat, from engines to the fate of the universe:
• Zeroth Law: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. This defines temperature and is why a thermometer works — it reaches the same temperature as what it touches.
• First Law (conservation of energy): the change in a system's internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system: ΔU = Q − W. Energy is never created or destroyed. You cannot get more energy out of an engine than you put in — no perpetual-motion machine 'of the first kind' can exist.
• Second Law (entropy): heat flows spontaneously only from hot to cold, and the total entropy (disorder) of an isolated system always increases. No engine can be 100% efficient — some energy must always be dumped as waste heat to a cold reservoir. This forbids a perpetual-motion machine 'of the second kind' and gives time its direction (the 'arrow of time').
• Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K), a perfect crystal's entropy approaches zero, and absolute zero itself is unreachable.
Practical machines: a heat ENGINE (car, power plant) takes heat from a hot source, converts SOME to work, and rejects the rest to a cold sink; the maximum possible (Carnot) efficiency is 1 − T_cold/T_hot (temperatures in Kelvin). A REFRIGERATOR or heat pump runs an engine backwards, using work (electricity) to pump heat from cold to hot — which is why the back of your fridge is warm and why it cannot cool a room with its door open (it dumps more heat than it removes). The Second Law is the ultimate reason energy 'costs' something and why efficiency can be improved but never reach 100%.

sections.heading: Heat Engines, Refrigerators, and the Carnot Limit
sections.body:
A heat engine is any device that converts a flow of heat from a hot reservoir to a cold one into useful mechanical work — a car engine, a steam turbine, a jet engine. Its efficiency is defined as η = W/Q_h, the work extracted divided by the heat energy drawn from the hot source. In 1824, a young French military engineer named Sadi Carnot proved a result so fundamental it predates the atomic understanding of heat entirely: no heat engine operating between two temperatures can ever exceed the efficiency η_max = 1 − T_c/T_h, where temperatures are measured in kelvin. Carnot died of cholera in 1832 at just 36, years before Clausius and Kelvin built the full theory of thermodynamics that would explain why his limit was unbreakable — yet his result still stands as an absolute ceiling, a direct consequence of the second law.

A gasoline engine with combustion gases reaching roughly 1,200°C (1,473 K) and exhausting near ambient temperature, 300 K, has a Carnot ceiling of η_max = 1 − 300/1473 ≈ 0.80, or 80%. Real engines achieve only about 25–35%, the gap consumed by friction, incomplete combustion, and heat lost through the engine block — a vivid illustration of just how far practical machines fall short of the thermodynamic ideal, and why 'perpetual improvement' in engine efficiency still has real headroom left even after a century of engineering.

Refrigerators and heat pumps run the same cycle in reverse, using work input to move heat from cold to hot (against its natural direction), characterized by a coefficient of performance COP = Q_c/W. A refrigerator holding its interior at 4°C (277 K) in a 20°C (293 K) kitchen has a Carnot-limit COP of 277/(293−277) ≈ 17 — real refrigerators typically manage only 2 to 4, again far below the theoretical ceiling, mostly due to irreversible heat exchange at the coils and compressor inefficiencies.

sections.heading: Entropy: The Statistical Meaning of the Arrow of Time
sections.body:
Beyond the macroscopic statement that 'heat flows from hot to cold' lies a deeper, statistical explanation for why the second law of thermodynamics is essentially unbreakable: entropy measures the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) consistent with a system's observable macroscopic state, formalized by Ludwig Boltzmann as S = k_B ln W, where W is that count of microstates and k_B is Boltzmann's constant. After Boltzmann's death in 1906, this exact equation was engraved on his tombstone in Vienna's Zentralfriedhof cemetery — a rare case of a single formula being judged worthy of standing as someone's epitaph.

The reason entropy tends to increase isn't a mysterious force pushing disorder — it's overwhelming probability. Shuffle a standard 52-card deck and there are 52! (52 factorial) possible orderings, roughly 8 × 10⁶⁷ — an incomprehensibly large number — yet only one of those arrangements is 'perfectly sorted by suit and rank.' A shuffled deck isn't disordered because some force made it so; it's disordered because there are astronomically more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, so a random shuffle lands on one almost with certainty. Gas molecules spreading to fill a room, ice melting into a warm glass of water, heat flowing from a hot object to a cool one — all of these happen because the 'spread out' or 'mixed' macrostate corresponds to vastly more microscopic arrangements than the concentrated one, not because any individual molecule is required to do anything in particular.

This statistical picture is also why the arrow of time feels one-directional: reversing any of these processes (unmixing cream from coffee, gas spontaneously collecting in one corner) is not physically forbidden at the level of any single collision — every microscopic interaction is time-reversible — but it is statistically so improbable for a macroscopic system that it has, for all practical purposes, never been observed to happen spontaneously.

sections.heading: Humidity, Dew Point, and Why Humid Heat Hits Harder
sections.body:
Relative humidity — the number quoted in every weather forecast — is the ratio of the actual water vapor pressure in the air to the maximum (saturation) vapor pressure the air could hold at that temperature, expressed as a percentage. Because warmer air can hold more water vapor before saturating, the SAME absolute amount of moisture in the air produces a HIGHER relative humidity reading on a cool morning than on a hot afternoon — which is why early morning grass is often dewy even on a day that later reads as comparatively dry. The dew point is the temperature at which the air's current moisture content would exactly saturate it; cool air down to that temperature (a cold glass of lemonade, the ground overnight) and water condenses out as dew, fog, or frost.

This connects directly to why humid heat feels so much more oppressive than dry heat at the identical air temperature. The body's primary cooling mechanism is evaporative: sweat absorbs roughly 2,400 kJ of latent heat for every kilogram evaporated at skin temperature (slightly higher than water's 2,260 kJ/kg value at its 100°C boiling point, since latent heat of vaporization rises somewhat as temperature falls), carrying that heat away from the skin as the sweat turns to vapor. But evaporation only proceeds efficiently when the surrounding air isn't already close to saturated with moisture — in high-humidity conditions, sweat simply can't evaporate as fast, so the body's main heat-shedding mechanism partially fails even though sweat production continues (or increases), leaving you drenched and still overheated. Endurance athletes can lose over a liter of sweat per hour in hot conditions; at 2,400 kJ/kg, that liter alone represents 2.4 megajoules of heat the body is trying — and in humid air, struggling — to shed.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: This experiment needs kitchen-level tools plus a couple of inexpensive extras from a hardware or general goods store.
ingredients: A digital instant-read thermometer or a lab-style glass thermometer, accurate to at least 1°C
A kitchen scale that reads in grams
Two or three disposable styrofoam cups (their poor thermal conductivity makes them a serviceable improvised calorimeter)
A metal object of unknown or to-be-verified composition — a large steel bolt, a lead fishing sinker, or an aluminum block, ideally 50-150 grams
A small pot and a stove or hot plate to bring water to a boil
Tongs or a slotted spoon (for safely transferring the hot metal)
A graduated cylinder or a measuring cup marked in milliliters, for measuring water volume
Oven mitts or a folded towel for handling hot cookware
Optional: a cheap digital hygrometer (temperature/humidity gauge) if extending into the humidity section above

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Find the Specific Heat of an Unknown Metal
sections.body: This is a classic calorimetry experiment — you'll use conservation of energy to back-calculate a material property from nothing but temperature readings, and then check your result against known values to identify (or verify) the metal.
steps: Weigh your metal object on the kitchen scale and record its mass, m_metal, in grams.

Measure out a known mass of room-temperature water into a styrofoam cup using the graduated cylinder — 1 milliliter of water equals almost exactly 1 gram, so 150 mL gives you 150 g of water directly. Record the water's starting temperature, T_i.

Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil and carefully lower the metal object in with tongs. Let it sit in the boiling water for at least 5 minutes so it fully reaches 100°C throughout (assuming standard sea-level atmospheric pressure).

Using tongs, quickly and carefully transfer the hot metal directly from the boiling pot into the styrofoam cup of room-temperature water — minimize delay to reduce cooling in transit. Wear oven mitts and keep the transfer path clear of skin.
Gently stir the water with the thermometer (without touching the cup's sides) and watch the temperature rise; record the highest (equilibrium) temperature it reaches, T_f.

Apply conservation of energy: the heat lost by the cooling metal equals the heat gained by the warming water (ignoring small losses to the cup and air): m_metal · c_metal · (100 − T_f) = m_water · c_water · (T_f − T_i), where c_water = 4.186 J/(g·°C).
Solve this equation for c_metal, the one unknown.

Compare your computed value against reference specific heats to identify the likely metal: aluminum ≈ 0.90 J/(g·°C), steel/iron ≈ 0.45-0.49 J/(g·°C), lead ≈ 0.13 J/(g·°C), copper ≈ 0.39 J/(g·°C). A result noticeably off from all of these usually means heat was lost during the transfer step — try again with a faster transfer or a better-insulated container.

Safety note: boiling water and hot metal are genuine burn hazards — use tongs, not fingers, for every step involving the heated object, and have an adult present if a younger student is running this experiment.

guides.title: Waves, Sound, Light & Optics
guides.summary: The anatomy of a wave and the wave equation, transverse versus longitudinal waves, how sound behaves and travels, the Doppler effect, the electromagnetic spectrum, reflection and refraction, lenses and mirrors, and how the eye and everyday optical devices form images.

sections.heading: What a wave is: anatomy and the wave equation
sections.body:
A wave is a disturbance that transfers ENERGY from one place to another WITHOUT transferring matter. A cork bobs up and down as ripples pass but does not travel with them; the water stays put while energy moves through it.
Key properties:
• Wavelength (λ, lambda): the distance between two consecutive identical points (e.g. crest to crest), in metres (m).
• Frequency (f): the number of complete waves passing a point per second, in hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 cycle/second.
• Period (T): the time for one complete wave, T = 1/f, in seconds.
• Amplitude (A): the maximum displacement from rest — it sets a wave's energy (louder sound, brighter light, bigger surf). Energy is proportional to amplitude squared.
• Speed (v): how fast the wave travels, in m/s.
The wave equation ties them together: v = f·λ. Speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Worked example: a musical note of frequency 440 Hz (concert A) travelling in air at 343 m/s has wavelength λ = v/f = 343/440 ≈ 0.78 m. For a fixed wave speed, higher frequency means shorter wavelength — a crucial relationship for both sound and light.

sections.heading: Transverse and longitudinal waves
sections.body:
Waves come in two geometric types, defined by how the medium moves relative to the wave's travel direction.
• Transverse waves: the medium oscillates PERPENDICULAR to the direction of travel. Picture shaking a rope up and down while the wave runs along it. Light and all electromagnetic waves, water surface waves, and waves on strings are transverse. They have crests (high points) and troughs (low points), and can be polarised (restricted to one vibration plane — the basis of polarised sunglasses and LCD screens).
• Longitudinal waves: the medium oscillates PARALLEL to the direction of travel, in a push-pull motion. Picture pushing and pulling a stretched spring (a Slinky) along its length. Sound waves are longitudinal, consisting of compressions (regions where particles bunch up, high pressure) and rarefactions (regions where they spread out, low pressure). Seismic P-waves are also longitudinal.
A key consequence: because longitudinal waves like sound need particles to compress and rarefy, they CANNOT travel through a vacuum — in space, no one can hear you scream. Transverse electromagnetic waves like light need no medium and cross empty space freely, which is why we see the Sun and distant stars.

sections.heading: Sound: how it travels and behaves
sections.body:
Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave produced by a vibrating source (vocal cords, a speaker cone, a guitar string) that pushes on the surrounding air. Our perception maps onto physics: pitch corresponds to frequency (high frequency = high pitch), and loudness corresponds to amplitude. The human ear typically hears 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; below is infrasound, above is ultrasound (used in medical imaging and sonar).
Speed of sound depends on the MEDIUM, and rises with stiffness and falls with density. In air at 20 °C it is about 343 m/s; it increases roughly 0.6 m/s per °C warmer. Strikingly, sound travels FASTER in denser-but-stiffer media: ~1480 m/s in water and ~5000 m/s in steel — about 15× faster than in air — because tightly bound particles pass the disturbance along quickly.
The loudness scale is logarithmic, measured in decibels (dB): 0 dB is the threshold of hearing, normal conversation ~60 dB, heavy traffic ~85 dB, a rock concert ~110 dB, and a jet engine ~140 dB. Every 10 dB increase is a tenfold jump in sound intensity. Safety note: prolonged exposure above ~85 dB causes permanent hearing damage; use ear protection around power tools, firearms and loud music.
Worked example — thunder distance: light from lightning reaches you almost instantly, but sound takes ~3 seconds per kilometre (343 m/s). Count the seconds between flash and thunder and divide by 3 for kilometres (or by 5 for miles): a 6-second gap means the strike was about 2 km away.

sections.heading: The Doppler effect, echoes and resonance
sections.body:
The Doppler effect is the change in a wave's observed frequency when the source and observer move relative to each other. As an ambulance approaches, its sound waves are 'squashed' to a shorter wavelength and higher pitch; as it passes and recedes, they stretch to a lower pitch — the familiar 'neeee-oww'. The source's actual pitch never changes; only what you hear does. The same effect on light lets astronomers measure how fast galaxies move: light from receding galaxies shifts toward longer (red) wavelengths — the 'redshift' — key evidence that the universe is expanding. Doppler radar uses it to measure vehicle speeds and storm winds.
Echoes are reflected sound. Bats, dolphins and sonar systems use echolocation: emit a pulse, time the echo's return, and compute distance as d = (v × t)/2 (halved because the sound travels there AND back). If an echo returns in 0.4 s in air, the reflecting surface is (343 × 0.4)/2 ≈ 69 m away.
Resonance occurs when a system is driven at its natural frequency, causing it to vibrate with large amplitude. A pushed swing timed to its natural rhythm goes higher; a wine glass shatters when a voice hits its resonant frequency; musical instruments amplify specific notes by resonating in their air columns or bodies. Resonance also has an engineering danger side — bridges and buildings must be designed so wind or footsteps do not drive them at a destructive resonant frequency.
